title: 106 years: remembering Dattopant Thengadi, and the hundredth post
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Born 10 November 1920: Thengadi's early life and learning, his ideas, and a closing reflection for the first hundred Sundays.
body:
*Photo: Dattopant Thengadi (1920-2004)*

Five days ago, on **10 November**, India marked **106 years** since the birth of **Dattopant Thengadi**, the founder of Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh. This is also the hundredth post in this Sunday series. It seems right to use the occasion to look at the man's early life and learning, the ideas he developed, and what the series has tried to do in his spirit. Our last Thengadi post, in October, looked at what he left behind. This one looks at how he became who he was.

## The boy from Arvi

Dattatreya Bapurao Thengadi was born on 10 November 1920 at Arvi in Wardha district, Maharashtra. His father, Bapurao Dajeebaa Thengadi, was an advocate, and his mother was Janaki Devi. He was already active as a schoolboy: at fifteen he was president of the Vanar Sena and of the student union of the municipal high school in Arvi. He went on to study law at Nagpur, taking an LLB, and he also did postgraduate studies at Morris College ([Wikipedia: Dattopant Thengadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dattopant_Thengadi)).

In 1942 he became a full-time pracharak of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. A tribute on the Thengadi archive records his postings as Kerala from 1942 to 1944, Bengal from 1945 to 1947 and Assam in 1948 and 1949, and notes that he helped set up the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad in 1949 ([Dattopant Thengadi Archive: An efficient organisation builder](https://dbthengadi.in/an-efficient-organisation-builder/)). Bengal was thus one of the first places where the young organiser worked, a fact of particular interest to readers in West Bengal.

## Learning the trade of the union

Thengadi did not begin as a trade unionist. Wikipedia records that he was an organising secretary of the Indian National Trade Union Congress in 1950 and 1951 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dattopant_Thengadi)). An article by a leader of the Swadeshi Jagran Manch says that, on the instruction of M. S. Golwalkar, he worked among labourers, joined the Congress-affiliated INTUC and later a communist-dominated postal and telegraph workers' union, and studied how unions worked ([Organiser, November 2025](https://organiser.org/2025/11/09/324888/bharat/birth-anniversary-of-dattopant-thengadi-embodiment-of-swadeshi-spirit/)). That article is advocacy by an associate of Thengadi's work, and its details should be read with that in mind, but the pattern is clear: he studied other unions closely before building his own.

The result was BMS, founded on 23 July 1955. The founding group gathered at Bhopal, and the organisation began without members, offices or funds, and was built up from local unions to national federations ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf)). The Thengadi archive describes him as the founder-president.

## Widening the circle

From the labour field he moved outwards. The Bharatiya Kisan Sangh was founded in 1979, the Samajik Samarasata Manch in 1983 and the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch in 1991, according to the Thengadi archive; the Swadeshi Jagran Manch article places the founding of the Kisan Sangh at Kota and the Swadeshi Manch at Nagpur on 22 November 1991 ([Dattopant Thengadi Archive](https://dbthengadi.in/an-efficient-organisation-builder/); [Organiser, November 2025](https://organiser.org/2025/11/09/324888/bharat/birth-anniversary-of-dattopant-thengadi-embodiment-of-swadeshi-spirit/)). The thread connecting them was his belief that the worker, the farmer and the consumer have common interests. In his 1986 booklet on consumers he argued that these groups are all exploited by middlemen and profiteers and that they should form a united front rather than be set against each other ([Consumer: A Sovereign without Sovereignty](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Consumer%20A%20Sovereign%20without%20Sovereignty.pdf)).

He also travelled to see other systems for himself. The archive records a 1969 visit to the Soviet Union and Hungary with a parliamentary delegation, an ILO conference in Switzerland and an anti-apartheid conference in Geneva in 1977, a 1979 study visit to Yugoslavia, the United States, Canada and Britain to look at labour movements, and a 1985 BMS delegation to China followed by an ILO regional conference in Jakarta ([Dattopant Thengadi Archive: Remembering Dattopant Thengadi](https://dbthengadi.in/remembering-shradheya-dattopant-thengadi/)). The BMS pamphlet records that BMS leads the Indian labour delegation to the International Labour Conference in Geneva each year ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf)), a tradition of looking outward that began early.

## Ambedkar and social harmony

A distinctive strand in his work was his respect for B. R. Ambedkar. Wikipedia lists Ambedkar, along with M. S. Golwalkar and Deendayal Upadhyaya, among his influences. The Thengadi archive records the release, on 16 October 2005, of his book on Ambedkar and the social revolution by the then RSS chief K. S. Sudarshan at Bhopal, which presents Ambedkar as a nationalist and describes his close relationship with Thengadi ([Dattopant Thengadi Archive](https://dbthengadi.in/remembering-shradheya-dattopant-thengadi/)). The Samajik Samarasata Manch and BMS's own Sarva Panth Samadar Manch, founded in 1994 to promote harmony among workers of all religions, reflect a similar concern for harmony across caste and faith ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf)).

## What these hundred Sundays covered

Our series has tried, in its own small way, to work in the same spirit of study and service. Looking back, the hundred posts have touched on these themes:

- **Law:** the four Labour Codes, wages, social security, safety and contracts.
- **The world:** the ILO, platform work standards, BRICS and international forums.
- **Workers left out:** scheme workers, gig workers, domestic and migrant workers.
- **Federations:** from railways and defence to beedi and fisheries.
- **Ideas:** *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit*, labourisation, Swadeshi, Samarasata.
- **People:** Thengadi Ji, Ambedkar, Gandhi, the new national team.

We have tried to keep to a simple rule: say what the sources say, name the sources, and mark clearly where something is opinion. If a post has fallen short of that, we want to hear about it.

## What he would want

Putting words in the mouth of a founder is a risk, so we will say only what the record supports. Those who knew him describe a man who preferred the background to the platform, who wrote over a hundred books and booklets in Hindi, Marathi and English, and who remained a full-time pracharak until his death ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf); [Gurumurthy, "A Tapasvi dies. Unnoticed"](https://dbthengadi.in/dattopant-thengadi-a-tapasvi-dies-unnoticed/)). If we take that example as a guide, the instruction for the rest of us is simple and old-fashioned: teach workers, serve the nation and remain simple. The work of explaining a new law to a contract worker, or helping a small union keep honest accounts, is exactly the kind of unglamorous work he did for decades.

## What next

This blog will continue, with a new article every Sunday at 7:00 am. Karyakartas can also post through the admin panel, using the **Write** page. We would particularly like to hear from State and district units about problems they face with the new rules, so that we can explain them. Suggestions for topics are welcome.

Thank you for reading.
